records.title: Show HN: OpenComputer – an open source alternative to Devin
records.author: iacguy
records.storyText:
Hi HN!

Utpal here, I'm one of the founders of OpenComputer.

OpenComputer is an open source cloud coding agent for teams that can run in your own cloud account (AWS, GCP, Azure).

We run the agent harness and the sandbox on the same durable VM (architecture in the docs [1]). First commit lands in 24s; the alternatives we benchmarked took 53-72s (benchmarks below [2]).

Two other choices:

- One VM per team, scalable horizontally. Sessions are isolated in git worktrees. - Session files are backed up to a repo after every turn, so any session can resume on another VM.

We noticed that past ~640 session-hours a month, one always-on 4 vCPU VM is cheaper than per-session E2B sandboxes, for example. So at scale, this setup would not only be faster than current SOTA coding agents, but also more cost-efficient.

Feel free to try via cloud for free [4] or self host. We would love any and all feedback, and happy to answer any questions! Full demo below [3].

[1]: https://docs.opencomputer.dev/getting-started/architecture [2]: https://opencomputer.dev/blog/cloud-agents-as-fast-as-local/ [3]: https://x.com/IgorZIJ/status/2121309785882591711 [4]: https://app.opencomputer.dev

records.author: grandimam
records.storyText:
When LLMs hands you a resume or pdf it carry markers of how it was made, including the source. You can't see them on the page but applicant tracking systems can read it.

So recruiters are flagging such profiles and rejecting them entirely. I had tested this across 40+ AI models (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, etc) to produce a resume and every single file carried a marker.

To solve this problem. I had built a free tool to show what your file says and gives you a cleaned version:

- Drop your resume and get a cleaned copy - Free, no account.

What it doesn't do: it won't rewrite your resume or make AI-sounding wording more human. It only deals with what's hidden in the file.

It's a simple tool, but it feels absolutely necessary now as more people are using AI for generating their entire resume or even editing them. I am the developer, happy to answer any questions.

records.title: Show HN: Musset, open-source Scrivener alternative with an AI that never writes
records.author: julienmarie
records.storyText:
I’m writing my first novel and could not find an app that fit my workflow: quiet like iA Writer, organized like Scrivener, and with AI so I can discuss my book while I write it. It allows me to feel less “alone” and have a sounding board while I write.

- A book is a folder of plain Markdown files. Musset commits to a git repo, tracks versions and drafts without you having to know git.

- Revisions are CriticMarkup inside the text. It manages docx revisions too, so your editor can edit a Word doc and you import their comments.

- PDFs are typeset using Typst, embedded in the app, following each language’s typographic rules.

- Spelling and grammar are checked using LanguageTool, also embedded.

- Mac/Word, WordStar, vi and Emacs keyboard modes.

The AI is optional and uses your Codex or Claude Code CLI. It comments, leaves margin notes, and checks continuity and your chapters against your style rules.

It’s GPL-3.0 and free during the beta. When or if it reaches 1.0, if there is sufficient interest, the idea is to make it a small one-time payment ($9.90). There is a paid sync service (git hosting) that lets you share a book with beta readers and editors.

Download: https://musset.app

I’d love to have some feedback!

records.title: Show HN: Lightweight FUSE-based encrypted, compressed filesystem for Linux
records.author: tgaloppo
records.storyText:
A personal project for digging deeper into Linux system programming, ObFUSEcate implements a file backed virtual block device that automatically performs compression and encryption as blocks are accessed. This virtual device can be mounted via FUSE (requiring no root privileges) to provide, effectively, a "live" compressed, encrypted archive.

Written in C++, and intended to have minimal dependencies, it has custom 32 bit arithmetic encoding/decoding, ChaCha20-Poly1305 authenticated encryption, and CRC8 + XOR parity error-correction.

Hi everyone,

Board is a way to create, deploy, and fund a trading bot in 10 seconds. My co-founders and I built Board out of our own necessity. Every time we had a new trading strategy, we would need to manually input it into our broker accounts and monitor the situation ourselves.

We looked at all of our trading strategies over the past 3 years and added everything to the board that would be required to rebuild them from scratch. records.title: Show HN: LarpLess, open-source study tracker detecting distractions locally
records.author: maergune
records.storyText:
I am ashamed to admit that I am one of those students who go to the library and get very little done (a.k.a. larping). It's very easy to get distracted if you have any electronic devices with you, but as a CS major, I can't just switch to pen and paper. That's why I started building this app called LarpLess with the help of a few friends.

LarpLess is a macOS/Windows app that checks your screen and camera with local AI to determine what you are studying or if you are distracted. Gives you a focus percentage at the end, with a breakdown of what you did during your session (Math, Physics, etc.)

Privacy is a big concern for an app like this, so it is open-source (AGPL 3.0) and uses locally run open-source models. It doesn't connect to the internet unless you want to check for updates or enable the friends feature (Disabled by default. You can make an account, add friends and see their shared study sessions/share your study sessions).

For the camera, it uses an object detection model, YOLO11n, to detect if there is a person and/or a phone at 1fps. For the screen, there are 2 options: the one we did first is reading window titles + a VLM on Ollama (default is qwen3-vl:2b), simple but power/RAM hungry. The one my friend added later can run on an average laptop easily. It takes less than a second for a verdict. It scores window titles + OCR text on the screen with MiniLM text embeddings and scores the screenshot with image embeddings using SigLIP 2. SigLIP 2 decides if the user is distracted, and MiniLM decides what they are working on. You can run the classifier-based mode on any modern laptop. If you want to use the VLM mode, you need a good GPU with enough VRAM (3GB+) to hold the model in it.

You can try it out by downloading the macOS version from GitHub (https://github.com/AlperErg/larpless/releases) or the Windows version from the Microsoft Store (https://apps.microsoft.com/detail/9nrvvphtmr9x).

I found it helpful for studying. I hope that you will as well. I'd appreciate it if you can give it a go and kindly share your thoughts.

p.s. My friend, who also works on this with me, posted about it before but without a description and not on Show HN, so I decided to post on Show HN with a good description.

records.title: Show HN: Jam – A music making game where you play gigs to earn studio gear
records.author: garrinm
records.storyText:
The idea comes from Chrome Music Lab, which was addictive and satisfying. I felt it could be that fun and easy to put down musical ideas and hear them grow into something more substantial. Simple at first, but with progressively more depth if the player wants to go there. That was the seed, and it spiraled from there into Jam.

You start with one instrument, and you write parts on a piano roll. Create your own music or play gigs (levels) to earn coins and buy more gear. Each gig is built around one musical idea, so you pick up some music knowledge as you go. Friends can join your studio with a link and write parts alongside you.

In my other Show HNs I've always come with my own code. In this case I didn't write the code, but I'm still proud of the outcome and I hope some of you will enjoy it too.

The audio code is Rust/WASM running in a worklet. This is the part I had prior experience in, and it's been fun getting that into a browser. The instruments are decent and the signal chains hold their own. The front end is the agent's own design in three.js. The optimization work there was interesting because of how busy the UI gets and how many elements come into view. I focused on measuring React renders per interaction, instruction counts for the audio engine, load times and frame times. The result is something that runs decently even on a phone.

The multiplayer side is simple. Each studio is a Cloudflare Durable Object that holds the song. Players connect to it over a WebSocket and send small actions (add a note, turn a knob). The object applies each action, stores the result and sends the updated session to anyone else in the room. This simple setup allows collaborative music making out of the gate, even though it's not the game's main focus (yet).

This is a beta: feedback, comments and criticisms are all welcome. You can get into the game with no signup, and if you want to save your progress you'll be prompted to enter an email address.

Hey HN, I have build a tool after my own job searching. You describe the job you want in a sentence, like "backend roles in Zurich, Python, no banks", and it searches the web and companies' own career pages for it. There is no bias, no curated lists, no promotion; only a pure and powerful search.

I wanted to get the real postings. The same jobs can show up to many boards and recruiter sites, often after it's closed. Don't you want to know this? Craoli tries to find the employer's own postings, shows one card for all the copies that exist out there, and keeps checking whether the job is still open.

Another issue I had was that one company while I submitted my job application, changed the job description, by adding one more requirement that was not there when I have applied!! Good luck proving that. Of course the recruiter brought this point for my rejection, that I was sure that it was not there when I applied. 7+ years of pre-sales is hard to miss on a job description when read.

There are some limits for now; career pages are read directly only for the common hiring systems; a custom site is only found through web search. And every search costs me real money, so you need an account, and free has 2 searches a month using a cheaper LLM model; the search costs the same. Additional classical features are there for you to discover, like tailored CVs and cover letters.

What I would like to know: the last time you looked for a job, what made you stop trusting a listing?

records.title: Show HN: ArkViz – AI generated software architecture diagrams
records.author: bofia
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I’m Bryant, founder of ArkViz (https://arkviz.io). ArkViz is a product to automatically generate architecture diagrams from your codebase using AI.

The vision behind ArkViz is to supercharge both AI agents and humans by providing AI agents deeper relational context using structured model diagram formats, and by providing humans with a rich visual representation you can interact with, with features like zooming, panning, search, and show composing files.

In this new age of AI, you can generate a structured model diagram from your codebase in seconds, quicker and better than a human. Not only can the generated diagram be a visual documentation tool for humans, AI agents can also benefit from the context of a pre-generated architecture diagram that lives alongside a project’s codebase. This concept has already been proven by context files like CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, ARCHITECTURE.md living in the root of your repository.

The differentiator between ARCHITECTURE.md and ArkViz is that ArkViz generates a structured model diagram of the system, while ARCHITECTURE.md is broader in scope and purely text. ArkViz aims to be a supplement to ARCHITECTURE.md to provide deeper understanding like how components are connected, which components live inside other components, which files compose a component.

—

Why ArkViz?

Software engineering teams often create diagrams to aid in the documentation of their software systems. They are incredibly useful for onboarding new engineers and understanding projects. However, they take time to create and maintain, so are often non-existent or out of date. ArkViz automates the creation and maintenance of software architecture diagrams, seamlessly and securely.

AI agents thrive when they have high quality context, including for architecture diagrams. However not all diagram formats out there are optimized for AI. A diagram showing connected systems and components can be represented in essentially 3 ways:

1. Unstructured drawing / canvas format (e.g. draw.io, Excalidraw, Figma, LucidChart)

  - Quick to get started but hard to maintain.
  - Good for brainstorming and whiteboarding
  - The format carries no semantic meaning and is basically represented by pixels, shapes, and vectors. Positioning is stored
  - Passing this to an AI agent as context has questionable value.
2. Structured diagramming formats (e.g. Mermaid, d2lang)

  - A level of abstraction higher than a 2D drawing canvas
  - Good for quick isolated diagram, like on GitHub
  - Represented by nodes and edges, nested hierarchies. Layout is generated
  - Better for AI agents, although they have to piece together the context, and might get confused by an inconsistency like duplicate naming
3. Structured modeling formats (e.g. Structurizr, LikeC4, IcePanel).

  - These have an underlying data model and single source of truth
  - High quality documentation, but hard to create and maintain
  - Represented by entities and relationships. Layout can be richer, like zooming into a component and seeing what's inside
  - Best for AI agents, since they have a single source of truth context
ArkViz currently uses LikeC4 for its diagram format, a modern, popular, and open-source architecture-as-code format that supports interactive diagrams. AI agents will be more trained with this than a proprietary format.

Why not roll my own solution with something like Claude Code? While Claude Code is a powerful AI coding harness, ArkViz provides seamless features you'd rather not spend time building like hosting diagrams, access control, scheduling automation, handling errors and retries, logs, connectors to GitHub. Additionally, ArkViz has battle-tested, optimized multi-pass prompts, validators, and guardrails for the specific purpose of AI generated architecture diagrams.

Take a look here: https://arkviz.io! Feedback greatly appreciated on which features you care about, and whether you think the value proposition is there.

records.title: Show HN: Klistra – Make launch videos and product demos, all in one AI studio
records.author: pvarghav
records.storyText:
I built Klistra: describe your video idea and add your logo, photos or other assets, Klistra designs and animates a video for you, exported for every screen size, with fonts, media and logos kept exact. Deterministic renders make features exact and isolated, allowing for superior control and iteration compared to diffusion models. Here's a short demo render where I made an ad for Klistra itself: https://app.klistra.ai/s/4EQoWCe37SkYz5nThgegzw

As a solo dev with a lot of projects going on, I found myself needing to make short promos or explainer videos. Not being familiar with animation software, I had the idea to use Claude to code up those videos and export them as video files. In the process of creating these clips I stumbled into a bunch of bugs and setup needed to make it work reliably. The list of features I wanted for better control and feedback kept growing and I needed to sign up for a bunch of services to get music, voiceovers and other media into my project. I couldn't find an existing service that had everything I wanted. Seeing these hurdles and that the technology was only easily accessible to people already confident with coding agents, I started working on Klistra, and a couple of months later I'm turning it into a service so you all can use it too.

The goal with Klistra was to include everything I missed in the manual workflow in an easy-to-use service with a nice UI, so people could focus on what they wanted the video to look like, not setting up the framework behind it. Klistra includes precise timeline control, media generation, built-in support to make animations match the rhythm of the background music, word extraction from voiceovers or songs, a dedicated iteration / feedback tool, website import and much more.

Something I knew I needed to get right was making it easy to iterate on small features of the video with precise control of what was being built. I designed Klistra so you first create a specification where you define scenes in detail, describe what you want shown and when, reference media or timestamps in-line, freely drag the timeline around and preview the result before letting a builder agent create the video. If you want to change something, the specification changes and the builder agent gets a diff of what changed. There is also a planner agent built into Klistra that helps create and edit the specification for you (which is what I use the most), while letting you turn to manual fine-tuning when needed.

Don't think of this as a replacement for diffusion models, if you want photorealistic images or videos they clearly do a better job. Klistra really shines when you need motion design and precise control, exact text with your fonts, media such as logos or voiceovers, animated UI that matches your apps and so on. Klistra does have built-in integrations for generating media from diffusion models, and combining the two technologies usually gets the best results.

Everything that costs money to run on Klistra, from machines to AI tokens, is paid for with credits included in a subscription or bought via one-time packs (Pro starts at $25/mo ($20 billed yearly) and packs at $12). Being a solo dev without funding, the budget wouldn't allow for a free tier with enough monthly credits for a real project. I instead decided to give the first 200 of you who sign up 350 free credits, enough for a simple video (the advanced tutorial used around 250 credits).

There is also a Claude Code integration in paid subscriptions, where your agent can act as a planner, convenient if you already have a project built with Claude that has all the context and you need an explainer, ad or social post. It also reduces credit spending if you're a heavy planner user.

- Tutorial, mostly using the planner: https://klistra.ai/docs/basic

- Advanced features and manual control: https://klistra.ai/docs/advanced

- More demos: https://klistra.ai/

Happy to hear what you think!

records.title: Show HN: Accounting built like Git, with files in your own storage
records.author: oskar77
records.storyText:
Lots of ways to do your accounting today with LLMs, but for some reason there is this expectation you are suppose to keep the old accounting software around? And it sort of makes sense, they vouch for the ledger integrity and keep the audit trail.

It reminded me of how things where like before git. You trusted the host not just to keep the data but to vouch for the versioning, and what git really did was move that last part into the data itself.

Accounting ledgers need integrity, in fact it is mandated by law in most places. Git buys integrity by publishing, because if you do not share your repo with anyone, you can always force push and rewrite the commit history and no-one would know. But your books are sensitive and cannot be published.

So I made git-style versioning for double-entry accounting. Entries gets hashed and timestamped, service checks for debit equals credit, and it ends up as json files you keep in your own S3 bucket. Not in a vendor database. For the hosted version the access keys to the buckets are encrypted with the user passkey / assistant OAuth, so the service cannot read anything at-rest.

For user convenience there is a hosted version where you do the books through MCP on whatever LLM you already use. The whole thing is so cheap to run, because the service does not store any sensitive data, so it is free, although you need an AI client with MCP support and an S3 bucket.

Hosted version: https://bobalice.com Code walkthrough: https://bobalice.com/docs/alice

records.title: Show HN: SwiphtNum 3.0 – native Mac statistics with SEM, SQL and scripting
records.author: shrun
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I build SwiphtNum, a statistics workspace written for the Mac in Swift, with the numeric kernels in C and Accelerate. There is no R or Python runtime inside; everything runs locally, and datasets never leave the machine.

What 3.0 changes:

- The SCL IDE. SCL is SwiphtNum's SPSS-like command language (169 commands). Scripts, SQL and results now share one window: any SQL statement is an SCL command, query results open in a Results tab, and the editor (a small C text engine) has autocomplete, folding, hover help and a command palette. SQLite, MySQL and PostgreSQL connect over SSL or SSH. - MANOVA: Pillai, Wilks, Hotelling and Roy, cell means, stepdown F and discriminant functions. - Ten interface languages, Text Size up to 200%, Differentiate Without Color and an Increase Contrast mode. - Statistical routines are tested against R and Python reference values in the test suite; the goldens are generated offline and checked in.

It also does CB-SEM and PLS-SEM on a visual canvas, 100+ procedures from one Analysis menu, APA 7 tables, and a spreadsheet with 191 Excel-compatible functions (dynamic arrays, LET, LAMBDA).

It needs macOS 14 or later and is a subscription ($4.99/month or $49.99/year, each with a free trial). Happy to answer anything about the stats engines, the SCL parser or the AppKit/SwiftUI split.

records.title: Show HN: Primeward – Exploring a stateful recurrence for the next prime
records.author: alexhr
records.storyText:
I’ve published Primeward, a Python research prototype. I started with a question: can we calculate the next prime from what we already know, rather than find it by brute force?

The implementation builds on known next-prime formulas. It uses a finite bound and interval arithmetic to extract the exact next prime from a stored arithmetic state, then updates that state and repeats.

It uses the Riemann zeta function and Euler products without assuming the Riemann Hypothesis.

The repo includes the implementation, an optimized version, correctness tests, sieve baselines, benchmarks, and research notes.

It’s currently slower than sieving. Building the initial state and maintaining enough numerical precision are expensive. I want to see how much we can reduce those costs while still calculating the exact next prime.

I’m interested in related work and ideas for reducing those costs.

github.com/alexhraber/primeward

records.title: Show HN: Straum – a Postgres materialized view that is never stale
records.author: jeeybee
records.storyText:
I've seen too many slow-log queries with a GROUP BY that makes Postgres blow up, so for the last two weeks or so I've been working on Straum. You declare the aggregates as a view, and Straum answers over HTTP (other transports might be added). I've been using the New York taxi dataset as a benchmark. On the heavier GROUP BYs I see about 1,000x to 5,000x. It's written in Rust (of course).

It leans on Postgres replication slots, logical or physical, to get its data. Postgres stays the source of truth.

Benchmark: https://janbjorge.github.io/straum/benchmark.html Repo: https://github.com/janbjorge/straum
